title: Subsurface Water Storage Capacity Mediates Precipitation‐Productivity Coupling Across Elevation in Western U.S. Montane Watersheds
content:
Abstract

Precipitation-productivity relationships in conifer forests remain poorly characterized despite their importance for predicting ecosystem responses to climate change. Here, we analyzed precipitation-productivity relationships across five snow-dominated watersheds in the western United States, focusing on the mediating role of subsurface water storage across elevation gradients. Using remote sensing-based productivity metrics and water balance analyses, mid-elevation (1,500–3,000 m) pine watersheds exhibited strong coupling between non-growing season (October-May) precipitation and subsequent productivity (r = 0.55–0.66, p < 0.05), primarily due to persistent moisture deficits. In contrast, high-elevation (>3,000 m) mixed conifer watersheds showed weak, statistically non-significant precipitation-productivity coupling, buffered by reliable replenishment of subsurface storage during the non-growing season. During recent droughts, growing season evapotranspiration at a high-elevation and a mid-elevation watershed was 17%–23% higher than in a year with similar antecedent precipitation, indicating shifts in water use strategies under stress. Regional analysis across the Southern Rocky Mountains and Sierra Nevada ecoregions confirmed these elevation-dependent patterns, with mid-elevation watersheds consistently showing the strongest precipitation sensitivity and high-elevation watersheds showing weaker coupling and consistent refilling of subsurface storage during the non-growing season. These high-elevation watersheds are therefore less vulnerable to interannual precipitation variability but may be sensitive to the timing of precipitation, earlier snowmelt, and longer-term depletion of subsurface ice storage that currently sustains baseflow in alpine catchments. These findings provide a framework for how climate change may impact forest productivity and water use differently across elevation gradients, highlighting local storage dynamics for assessing forest vulnerability to changes in water availability and developing targeted management strategies.
